# The problem {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## A hospital group asks…

> Does the new treatment reduce the hazard of readmission-or-death — **at every site**?

- 40 hospital sites, 2,000–10,000 patients each, ~50 lab values per patient
- Per site: Cox model `Surv(time, event) ~ treatment + age + sex + comorbidity`
- Uncertainty: percentile CI from **bootstrap resamples** per site

```{r}
bootstrap_site <- function(site_df, n_boot = 1000) {
  formula <- survival::Surv(time, event) ~ treatment + age + sex + comorbidity
  log_hr <- vapply(seq_len(n_boot), function(b) {
    idx <- sample.int(nrow(site_df), replace = TRUE)
    stats::coef(survival::coxph(formula, data = site_df[idx, ]))[["treatmentnew"]]
  }, numeric(1))
  data.frame(site = site_df$site[1], hr = exp(median(log_hr)), ...)
}
```

`R/01_simulate_cohort.R`, `R/functions.R`

## It worked with 200 resamples…

```{r}
system.time(bootstrap_site(one_site, n_boot = 200))   # the test run
```

```
Test run: 200 resamples of one site (7589 patients): 4.1 s
Production: 5000 resamples x 40 sites: ~45 minutes (0.8 hours) on one core
```

- Fine for testing; the real analysis needs **25× more resamples × 40 sites** (and the next cohort is bigger)
- Every resample is independent → **embarrassingly parallel**
- One task = **100 resamples of one site** → 5,000 resamples = 2,000 tasks of the same kind

`R/02_serial_baseline.R`

# Which tool when? {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What does this job need?

```{mermaid}
%%| eval: true
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 9
%%| fig-height: 4
flowchart LR
  A["Too slow?"] -->|"runs once,<br/>done overnight"| B["Submit <b>one</b> job<br/>(sbatch / Workbench Job)<br/>and do something else"]
  A -->|"runs often or<br/>blocks you"| C{"Many independent<br/>pieces?"}
  C -->|yes| D["<b>CPUs</b>: mirai daemons<br/>(this workshop)"]
  C -->|no| E{"Large dense linear algebra,<br/>boosted trees, deep learning?"}
  E -->|yes| F["<b>GPU</b> candidate —<br/>measure it (see the end)"]
  E -->|no| G["<b>Profile the code</b>,<br/>or more cores on one node"]
```

The cheapest speed-up is often **not** parallel. Every branch starts with **one measured task**.

## Optimise, parallelise, or let it run?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Let it run** when it runs once and finishes overnight — your time costs more than CPU time

**Parallelise** when there are many independent pieces and you'll rerun it (new data, new `n_boot`, reviewers…)

**Optimise first** when one piece is slow and you'll run it thousands of times
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Our own task, profiled with `Rprof()` / profvis:

- 42% of the time in `[.data.frame`: every resample copies **all 58 columns**, the model uses 5
- Keep 7 columns → **1.65× faster**, same hazard ratios, 8× less data to ship
- That's 1.65× on *every* node you'll ever use — for free
:::
::::

# mirai in 7 minutes {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Daemons + map

```{r}
library(mirai)
daemons(8)                                   # 8 persistent R workers

site_list <- split(cohort, cohort$site)
everywhere({}, site_list = site_list,        # shared data: once per daemon
           bootstrap_site = bootstrap_site)
tasks <- make_chunks(site_list, n_boot = 5000, chunk = 100)   # 2,000 rows: site, n_boot
draws <- mirai_map(tasks, bootstrap_chunk)[.progress]         # one row = one task
res   <- combine_chunks(tasks, draws, site_list)              # one row per site

daemons(0)                                   # always clean up
```

- Daemons start **empty**: no packages, no globals
  - packages: namespace-qualify inside the function (`bootstrap_site()` calls `survival::coxph()`), or `everywhere(library(survival))`
  - objects: pass them per task (`tasks` columns), via `.args`, or **once per daemon** with `everywhere()`
- Dispatcher hands tasks out FIFO as daemons become free
- `daemons(seed = 42)` → reproducible RNG regardless of how many daemons

## Same code, different place

```{r}
# laptop
daemons(8)

# SLURM: each daemon is one sbatch job that dials back to this session
daemons(8, url = host_url(), remote = cluster_config(
  command = "sbatch",
  options = "#SBATCH --mem=???\n#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=???\n#SBATCH --time=???"
))
```

The `mirai_map()` call does not change.

**But what goes into `???`**

# With great power comes great responsibility {background-color="#8e2c2c"}

## Why it matters

- `daemons(200, remote = cluster_config())` is one line — and 200 jobs in the queue
- Ask for **too much**: idle cores and RAM blocked for your colleagues, longer queue waits for *you* (the scheduler has to find bigger holes)
- Ask for **too little**: OOM-killed daemons, `TIMEOUT`, nodes oversubscribed
- Neither shows up as an R error you'd notice at once

**Rule: measure one task before you scale to N.**

## Profile one task, the way it will run

```{r}
profile_task <- function(fun, ..., interval = 0.1) {
  mirai::daemons(1, .compute = "profile")              # ONE fresh local daemon
  on.exit(mirai::daemons(0, .compute = "profile"))
  pid <- mirai::mirai(Sys.getpid(), .compute = "profile")[]
  res <- syrup::syrup(                                  # snapshot `ps` every 0.1s
    mirai::mirai(do.call(fun, args), .args = list(fun = fun, args = list(...)),
                 .compute = "profile")[],
    interval = interval)
  tidy_syrup(res, pid = pid)                            # keep daemon + its children
}

prof <- profile_task(bootstrap_chunk, site = "site_31", n_boot = 100,   # ONE task
                     helpers = list(site_list = site_list, bootstrap_site = bootstrap_site))
```

- Same code path as on the cluster (serialisation, fresh process, shared data on the daemon)
- Profile the **largest** task — memory must fit the worst case
- Fixed task size → **one profile is valid for any `n_boot`**: more resamples = more tasks, not bigger ones
- [syrup](https://simonpcouch.github.io/syrup/) sees *all* R processes on the machine → filter by PID

`R/03_profile_one_task.R`

## The well-behaved task

![](../results/profile_good.png){height=480}

One chunk (100 resamples, largest site): 2.7 s, flat ~375 MB (incl. the shared `site_list`). CPU a flat 100% → **1 core, small memory**

## Gotcha 1: memory that grows with the work

```{r}
profile_task(bootstrap_site, site_df = largest_site, n_boot = 1000, keep_fits = TRUE)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](../results/profile_fits.png)
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
- Same task, same 1,000 resamples
- Flat at ~230 MB vs. a ramp to ~1.75 GB (~1.5 MB per kept fit)
- Memory scales with resamples **per task**: chunks of 100 bound it, one 5,000-resample task would need ≈ 8 GB
- **Fix the code**, don't just ask for more RAM
:::
::::

## Gotcha 2: hidden parallelism

```{r}
bootstrap_site(..., n_cores = parallel::detectCores())   # a "helpful" colleague
```

![](../results/profile_nested.png){height=340}

`detectCores()` on a compute node = **all cores of the node**, not your allocation. 8 daemons × 64 forks.

In a 1-CPU job on our cluster: `parallel::detectCores()` → **4**, `parallelly::availableCores()` → **1**.

## Gotcha 2: what to do

- CPU % well above 100 → the task uses more than one core
- **Never size parallelism with `parallel::detectCores()`**: it counts the hardware, not what you are allowed to use
- Either request `--cpus-per-task=k` **and** respect it:
  ```{r}
  n_cores <- parallelly::availableCores()   # honours SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, cgroups, CPU affinity, ...
  ```
- Or, for embarrassingly parallel work: keep tasks single-threaded and let mirai parallelise
- Same story for multithreaded BLAS / OpenMP / data.table → set `OMP_NUM_THREADS`
  (on our cluster, openblas-pthread made the "well-behaved" task use ~350% CPU for **zero** speed-up)
- Caveat: forked children share memory pages — summing RSS over-counts

## Gotcha 3: shipping more than you need

```{r}
# whole cohort to every task, filter inside
mirai_map(site_ids, function(id) bootstrap_site(cohort[cohort$site == id, ]),
          .args = list(cohort = cohort))
```

| | serialised per task | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|
| whole cohort | ~90 MB | ~375 MB |
| one site (`split()` first) | ~4 MB | ~230 MB |

×40 tasks, over the network, held in every daemon.

Hidden passenger: a function defined *inside* another function ships that function's environment with every task. In our granularity test: 900 KB per task × 40,000 tasks ≈ 35 GB → session killed. Define task functions at top level.

## From measurements to `#SBATCH`

```{r}
p <- summarise_profile(prof_good)   # wall_s, peak_rss_mb, mean_cpu_pct, ...

resources <- list(
  cpus   = max(1, round(p$mean_cpu_pct / 100)),
  mem_mb = ceiling(p$peak_rss_mb * 1.5 / 256) * 256,          # 1.5x headroom
  time_s = rate * N_BOOT * sum(site_sizes) / N_DAEMONS * 2 + 300   # total work, 2x + start-up
)
cat(slurm_options(resources, partition = "compute"))
```

```
#SBATCH --job-name=mirai-coxboot
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=768M
#SBATCH --time=0-00:16:58
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
```

Limits apply **per daemon** (one sbatch job each).

## Memory per core: match the node shape

Node ratio = RAM ÷ cores, e.g. 8 cores, 32 GB → **4 GB per core**

- Task needs ≤ the ratio → SLURM can fill every core of a node
- Task needs more → memory runs out before cores do: the remaining cores sit idle *and* are blocked for others

Our nodes: 4 cores, 14.8 GB → **3.7 GB per core** (`DefMemPerCPU=3700`)

| task | `--mem` | daemons per node | idle cores |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bootstrap_chunk()` (100 resamples) | 768 MB | 4 | 0 |
| `keep_fits = TRUE`, 5,000 resamples | ~12 GB | 1 | 3 |

```bash
sinfo -N -o "%N %c %m"                       # cores and memory (MB) per node
scontrol show config | grep DefMemPerCPU
```

# Launching on SLURM {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Right-sized daemons

```{r}
daemons(
  n        = 8,
  url      = host_url(),                       # compute nodes dial back here
  remote   = cluster_config(command = "sbatch",
                            options = slurm_options(resources, partition = "compute"),
                            rscript = RSCRIPT),
  seed     = 42,
  idletime = 5 * 60 * 1000,                    # idle daemon exits -> frees allocation
  walltime = (resources$time_s - 120) * 1000   # stop before SLURM kills us
)
wait_for_daemons(8)                            # jobs may sit in the queue

everywhere({}, site_list = site_list, bootstrap_site = bootstrap_site)
draws <- mirai_map(make_chunks(site_list, 5000, 100), bootstrap_chunk)[.progress]
daemons(0)
```

- Sort tasks **largest first** → a big chunk doesn't finish last on its own
- Shared data via `everywhere()`: 2,000 tasks each carrying their site's data would queue ~4 GB in *your* session
- Compute nodes need network access to the Workbench session and the same R packages

`R/04_launch_slurm.R`

## Alternative: the Workbench Launcher

```{r}
daemons(
  n      = 8,
  url    = host_url(),
  remote = http_config(cpus = resources$cpus, memory = resources$mem_mb),
  seed   = 42
)
```

- Workbench submits the jobs for you (admin-configured cluster / resource profiles)
- Same lesson: pass the **measured** `cpus` / `memory`, not the biggest profile

## Close the loop: requested vs. used

```bash
sacct --name=mirai-coxboot -S today --units=M \
      --format=JobID,State,ReqCPUS,ReqMem,Timelimit,Elapsed,TotalCPU,MaxRSS
seff <jobid>
```

- Usage (`TotalCPU`, `MaxRSS`) is on the `.batch` step line, not the job line
- `MaxRSS` ≪ `ReqMem` → lower `--mem` next time
- `TotalCPU` ≈ `Elapsed × ReqCPUS` → the cores were actually used
- `OUT_OF_MEMORY` / `TIMEOUT` → back to profiling

```{r}
for (n in c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)) {
  start_daemons(n, resources, ...)                        # queue time measured separately
```

`R/05_scaling.R`, `R/06_plot_scaling.R`

## Speedup

![](../results/scaling_speedup.png){height=480}

## Efficiency

![](../results/scaling_efficiency.png){height=360}

- One site per task would hit a floor: never faster than the **largest site** (dotted line) → chunks avoid it
- Beyond ~70% efficiency loss, extra daemons are mostly idle allocations
- On a busy cluster, **queue time** for many jobs can outweigh the compute gain

## Why 100 resamples per task?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Same work (40 sites × 1,000 resamples), different task sizes. Efficiency vs. 1 daemon:

| one task = | tasks | 8 | 24 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 site | 40 | 87% | 80% | **65%** |
| 100 resamples | 400 | 90% | 88% | **88%** |
| 10 resamples | 4,000 | 89% | 87% | 87% |
| 1 resample (~13 ms) | 40,000 | 86% | 84% | 84% |

```{r}
everywhere({}, site_list = site_list)   # ship shared data once per daemon
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
- **Too coarse**: few, unequal tasks → the largest one is the floor (27 s at 24 *and* 30 daemons)
- Split big tasks into similar-sized chunks, combine afterwards → 65% → 88%
- **Too fine**: every task pays dispatch + result overhead (~0.1 ms in mirai). 13 ms tasks still lose ~4%; sub-ms tasks → group them into chunks
- Rule of thumb: **≥ 10× more tasks than daemons**, each ≥ ~0.1 s → our choice: 100 resamples
- `R/08_granularity.R`
:::
::::

# Quarto + SLURM {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Pattern: compute in a job, render in seconds

```bash
sbatch fit_job.sh              # R/04_launch_slurm.R: 2,000 tasks on SLURM daemons -> saveRDS()
quarto render report.qmd       # the .qmd only does readRDS(): renders anywhere, in seconds
```

```{r}
hr <- readRDS("results/site_hazard_ratios.rds")      # in report.qmd
```

- Rerendering for a typo shouldn't rerun 45 CPU-minutes
- In a Quarto project: `execute: freeze: auto` keeps computed results until the code changes; `cache: true` per chunk
- Or render the whole document as a job: `sbatch -c 4 --mem=4G --wrap 'quarto render report.qmd'`

## Where does my Quarto code run?

8 tasks with `future_map()`, `plan(multisession, workers = availableCores())` · measured with `quarto-demo/`

::: {style="font-size: 72%;"}
| started as | runs in | gets | workers | time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| console ("Run All") | session job | 4 CPU, 4 GB | 4 | 4.8 s |
| `quarto render` in session | **same** session job | 4 CPU, 4 GB | 4 | 4.4 s |
| `sbatch -c 4` render | its own job | 4 CPU, 4 GB | 4 | 4.3 s |
| `sbatch -c 1` render | its own job | **1 CPU**, 2 GB | **1** | 8.4 s |
| session render + daemons | session + 4 daemon jobs | 4 CPU, 4 GB | 4 | 4.1 s |
| `sbatch -c 1` render + daemons | 1-CPU job + 4 daemon jobs | 1 CPU, 2 GB | 4 | 4.1 s |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,30,18,11,11]"}
:::

- Rendering starts a new R process **inside the allocation that started it** — `detectCores()` said 4 every time
- Big parallel work in a report: keep the render job small and send the work to daemons (last row)

# Wrap-up {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Checklist before `daemons()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Before you launch**

0. Decide: one job overnight, many CPUs, or a GPU?
1. Profile **one** task (the largest); fixed task size
2. Memory flat? CPU ≈ 100%? Else fix the code
3. Ship only what tasks need; task functions at top level
4. Return only what post-processing needs
5. `--mem`, `--cpus-per-task`, `--time` with headroom; memory per core ≤ node RAM ÷ cores
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**When you run**

6. `idletime` / `walltime`; `daemons(0)` when done
7. Check `sacct` / `seff`, then refine
8. Pick `n` from the scaling curve
9. ≥ 10× more tasks than daemons, each ≥ ~0.1 s
:::
::::

## Same daemons, other front-ends

Here one task = one whole site (40 **unequal** tasks):

```{r}
start_daemons(8, resources, ...)    # = daemons(8, url = host_url(), remote = cluster_config(...))

purrr::map(site_list, purrr::in_parallel(                     # purrr >= 1.1
  \(d) bootstrap_site(d, n_boot = 5000), bootstrap_site = bootstrap_site))

future::plan(future.mirai::mirai_cluster)                     # furrr, future.apply, doFuture, ...
furrr::future_map(site_list, bootstrap_site, n_boot = 5000,
                  .options = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE))

cl <- make_cluster(8, url = host_url())                       # base parallel: parLapply(), ...
launch_remote(cl, remote = cluster_config(...))              # one sbatch job per node
```

- The **daemons** are what SLURM sizes → profiling and `#SBATCH` lessons carry over unchanged
- `in_parallel(...)` = ship only what you need, just like `.args`
- `make_cluster(8, remote = cluster_config(...))` infers *1* node from the config → `parLapply()` runs serially (~6× slower here). Check `length(cl)`!
- `R/07_other_frontends.R`

## Static chunks vs. one task at a time

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
40 sites, 8 daemons, same workers:

| front-end | default | one at a time |
|---|---|---|
| `mirai_map()` / purrr | **~18 s** | (default) |
| furrr | 28 s | **18 s** |
| `parLapply()` | 27 s | **17 s** |
| crew.cluster | | 21 s (incl. starting workers) |

```{r}
furrr_options(scheduling = Inf)
parLapply(cl, x, f, chunk.size = 1)   # or clusterApplyLB()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- furrr and `parLapply()` split the work into **one chunk per worker, up front**
- Sites sorted largest first → chunk 1 gets the 5 biggest (43k rows), chunk 8 the 5 smallest (10k rows)
- 7 workers finish early and wait — idle, but still allocated
- mirai / purrr hand out **one task at a time** → right for unequal tasks
:::
::::

## crew / crew.cluster (and targets)

```{r}
controller <- crew.cluster::crew_controller_slurm(
  workers = 8, seconds_idle = 300,
  options_cluster = crew.cluster::crew_options_slurm(
    partition = "compute", cpus_per_task = 1,
    memory_gigabytes_per_cpu = 0.5, time_minutes = 30
  )
)
targets::tar_option_set(controller = controller)
```

- crew launches and **auto-scales** its own mirai daemons as one SLURM **job array**
- … but the per-worker cpus / memory / time still come from **your profile** (from 03: 1 CPU, 768M per worker)
- `memory_gigabytes_per_cpu` → think node shape (≤ 3.7 GB per core here)

# GPUs: when do they help? {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## GPUs: what they buy *us*

55 predictors, 2M patients (Stan: 500k, 1 chain) · CPU: m7a · GPU: NVIDIA T4 · same answers in every case

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
| | CPU | GPU | gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| xgboost, 200 trees | 13.3 s | 3.8 s | **3.5×** |
| … via tidymodels `boost_tree()` | 19.2 s | 9.0 s | 2.1× |
| 8192² matrix multiply | 3.6 s | 0.29 s | **12×** |
| logistic GLM: `glm()` vs. cuda.ml | 13.4 s | 9.2 s | 1.5× |
| … own torch IRLS, fp64 / fp32 | 11.6 s | 4.3 / 0.95 s | 3× / 14× |
| Bayesian logistic GLM: CmdStan · brms (OpenCL) | 373 · 389 s | 63 · 34 s | **6× · 11×** |
| `coxph()` 2M rows · `glmer()` 500k rows | 6.3 · 7.5 s | no GPU path | — |

: {tbl-colwidths="[52,16,18,14]"}
:::

`R/09_gpu_benchmarks.R`, `R/10_cmdstan_opencl.R`

## When is a GPU worth it?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Worth trying**

- Boosted trees on large data: `device = "cuda"` (one `set_engine()` argument in tidymodels)
- Deep learning: torch, tensorflow/keras
- Large dense linear algebra
- cuda.ml: GPU engines for `logistic_reg()`, `rand_forest()`, SVMs
- Stan / brms GLM likelihoods (`bernoulli_logit_glm`, `normal_id_glm`, …): `brm(..., opencl = opencl(c(0, 0)))`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Don't bother**

- Cox, lme4 / glmmTMB: no GPU path
- Anything that fits in seconds
- Many small fits (one Cox fit here: 0.04 s) → **CPUs in parallel**
- brms / Stan models outside those functions: OpenCL speeds up "only some Stan functions" (brms docs)
:::
::::

## Before you switch to a GPU

- **Precision**: a T4 is fast in fp32, slow in fp64 — yet Stan's fp64 GLM still ran 6–11× faster. Measure, don't guess; check the answers
- **Setup cost**: GPU xgboost isn't on CRAN, torch needs its CUDA build, cuda.ml downloads 1.6 GB
- **The CPU side still matters**: our GPU node has 2 vCPU — tidymodels' data prep took longer than the GPU fit
- **brms gotcha**: after a CPU fit of the same model, add `stan_model_args = list(force_recompile = TRUE)` — or the cached CPU binary is reused and the chain fails
- **Same responsibility**: `#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1`, profile with `nvidia-smi` — GPU memory is the new `--mem`

# Appendix {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## The simulated cohort {.scrollable}

`R/01_simulate_cohort.R` calls this (from `R/functions.R`) and saves `data/cohort.rds`:

```{r}
cohort <- simulate_cohort(n_sites = 40)   # seed = 2026 -> same data every time
```

```{r}
simulate_cohort <- function(n_sites = 40, min_patients = 2000, max_patients = 10000,
                            n_biomarkers = 50, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  site_sizes <- round(stats::runif(n_sites, min_patients, max_patients))
  n <- sum(site_sizes)

  site       <- rep(sprintf("site_%02d", seq_len(n_sites)), times = site_sizes)
  site_idx   <- rep(seq_len(n_sites), times = site_sizes)
  age        <- round(stats::rnorm(n, 65, 12))
  sex        <- factor(sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE))
  comorbidity <- stats::rpois(n, 1.5)                 # Charlson-like index
  treatment  <- factor(stats::rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), labels = c("standard", "new"))

  site_log_hr   <- stats::rnorm(n_sites, log(0.75), 0.15)   # true per-site effect
  site_baseline <- stats::rnorm(n_sites, log(0.02), 0.3)

  lp <- site_baseline[site_idx] +
    site_log_hr[site_idx] * (treatment == "new") +
    0.03 * (age - 65) + 0.2 * (sex == "M") + 0.25 * comorbidity
  event_time  <- stats::rexp(n, rate = exp(lp))
  censor_time <- stats::runif(n, 0, 60)                # months of follow-up

  cohort <- data.frame(
    patient_id  = seq_len(n),
    site        = site,
    age         = age,
    sex         = sex,
    comorbidity = comorbidity,
    treatment   = treatment,
    time        = pmin(event_time, censor_time),
    event       = as.integer(event_time <= censor_time)
  )

  biomarkers <- matrix(stats::rnorm(n * n_biomarkers), ncol = n_biomarkers,
                       dimnames = list(NULL, sprintf("lab_%02d", seq_len(n_biomarkers))))
  cbind(cohort, biomarkers)
}
```
